child_drafts.description_long: At a February 12, 2026 event hosted by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum called the energy transition an ideological “fantasy” and questioned climate projections. E&E News reported that he described climate forecasts as based on incomplete data and likened belief in the transition to a “semi-religion.” The article also records his comments on the administration’s planned critical-mineral reserve, Project Vault: Burgum suggested that it might expand if market demand justified more investment. E&E News situated the speech on the same day the administration announced repeal of the EPA endangerment finding, a policy that had underpinned rules limiting greenhouse-gas emissions. Those details describe the remarks and their reported policy context; they do not establish that the speech itself changed climate policy or authorized a lease. The NPR-A auction took place separately on March 18, 2026, so its bid totals and acreage belong in a distinct event record.

child_drafts.description_long: On March 18, 2026, the Interior Department held an oil and gas lease sale in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. The department reported that 11 companies bid on 187 of the 625 tracts offered, covering about 1.335 million acres, and that the sale generated $163,696,722 in receipts. Interior called it the reserve’s highest-revenue sale, the sale with the most tracts receiving bids, and the second-largest by acreage. It was the first NPR-A sale since 2019 and the first under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Interior stated that Alaska would receive nearly $82 million, half the receipts, with some proceeds benefiting North Slope communities. The same release describes other administration actions affecting the reserve, including rescinding the 2024 leasing rule and adopting an activity plan reopening nearly 82 percent of the reserve to leasing. Those actions provide context but are distinct from this single-day auction. The page does not support the original card’s unrelated royalty-rate or congressional-criticism claims.

child_drafts.title: Gabbard Fires National Intelligence Council Acting Chairman and Deputy (May 2025)
child_drafts.description_short: Gabbard Fires National Intelligence Council Acting Chairman and Deputy (May 2025).
child_drafts.description_medium: Tulsi Gabbard removed National Intelligence Council acting chair Michael Collins and deputy Maria Langan-Riekhof in May 2025, according to The Washington Post. The removals followed an assessment that contradicted the administration’s stated rationale for deportations; their direct role in drafting that assessment was unclear. The assessment was dated April 7 and was later partially declassified.
child_drafts.description_long: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard removed National Intelligence Council acting chair Michael Collins and his deputy, Maria Langan-Riekhof, in May 2025, The Washington Post reported. Their departures came about a week after the council produced a partially declassified assessment stating that Venezuela’s government was most likely not directing the Tren de Aragua gang’s activity in the United States. That assessment undercut a rationale the Trump administration had used for invoking the Alien Enemies Act to deport alleged gang members. The Post said it was unclear whether Collins or Langan-Riekhof had a direct role in preparing the assessment, which was attributed to a National Intelligence Officer for the Western Hemisphere. The intelligence office spokesperson said Gabbard was working with Trump to end politicization of the intelligence community; lawmakers criticized the removals and warned they could chill independent analysis. The event should be stated as personnel removals following the report, while avoiding a definitive causal claim absent documentation.

child_drafts.description_long: The CIA terminated a number of recent hires in early March 2025 as part of a review of probationary employees, Reuters reported. Three people familiar with the matter said the dismissals affected more than a few employees, but the agency did not disclose a total. A CIA spokesperson said the agency was reviewing personnel in their first two years of service and that some reviews would result in termination. The employees worked across several portfolios, and a person familiar with the matter cited performance issues as the stated basis for some terminations. Reuters also reported, based on an unnamed source, that congressional intelligence committees had not been informed when the dismissals began, despite such notification being customary. The agency’s announcement supports a discrete staffing action, but the article does not verify a specific number or that all probationary officers were fired. The held language “mass firing” overstates the public evidence; claims about required notification and national-security effects should be attributed to the cited source or experts.

corrected_draft.description_long: On February 25, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a memorandum to the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy and the Attorney General, and to the directors of OMB, National Intelligence, CIA and OPM. GovInfo republishes the text but notes that an original was unavailable to it for verification. The held entry’s March 14 executive-order date and instrument are therefore inaccurate; this was a February 25 presidential memorandum.

corrected_draft.description_long: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” during a dispute over the administration’s effort to freeze federal funding. That day, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the administration’s request for an immediate administrative stay of a lower-court order blocking the broad freeze. The appellate panel said it was uncertain what standards governed the requested stay and noted that the administration had not cited authority supporting it. The court left the district judge to clarify the scope of the earlier order and said it would consider a later request for a stay pending appeal. ABC reported that the administration argued the order improperly constrained executive spending authority, while state plaintiffs said a renewed freeze would harm recipients of federal funding. Trump’s brief assurance was made in this litigation context. It contradicts the held card’s claim that he declared he was not bound by court orders; the evidence supports recording the February statement and court response, not the alleged March declaration.
